Field surveys of the Ember parrotfish, Scarus rubroviolaceus, in the northwestern Hawaiian Islands have provided key insights into its size structure. The total length at which this species attains puberty was estimated at 35 cm [Lp = 35 cm], a value derived from extensive gonadal examination of captured specimens. In contrast, the ultimate total length, representing the maximum size attainable under favorable conditions, reaches approximately 70 cm [Li = approximately 70 cm]. This substantial growth potential places Scarus rubroviolaceus among the larger members of the scarine lineage, with individuals frequently exceeding 60 cm in protected reef environments. The length-based estimates of maturation and maximum size are critical for understanding the species' vulnerability to fishing pressure, as size-selective harvest can truncate age structure and reduce reproductive output within the population. Data from adjacent regions suggest that these size benchmarks are relatively consistent across the species' range, although local variation in food availability and thermal regimes may influence asymptotic size to some degree.

From the same specimens used to assess maturity, body mass data were collected to establish length-weight relationships. The wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the 35 cm length threshold, was calculated at 788 grams [Wwp = 788 grams]. This value is derived from the general length-weight equation for the species, which conforms to an allometric exponent typical of reef fishes. At the upper end of the size spectrum, the ultimate wet weight is substantially greater, reaching approximately 6,770 grams [Wwi = approximately 6,770 grams] for individuals that achieve the maximum recorded length. This dramatic increase in mass from puberty to senescence reflects the continued somatic investment that occurs after sexual maturation, a common pattern among iteroparous teleosts. The mass range of the Ember parrotfish, from a few hundred grams at first maturity to several kilograms as a large adult, imposes distinct metabolic and ecological constraints. Larger individuals, for instance, possess greater bioerosion capacity through their feeding activities, playing a pivotal role in the geomorphology of carbonate reef systems.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was approximately 12% [GSI = approximately 12%] under the ambient thermal conditions typical of the species' spawning habitat, approximately 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. The spawning season is protracted in this species, and field observations indicate that individual females likely participate in multiple spawning events each year, with an assumed frequency of three spawnings annually. This pattern may buffer the population against stochastic recruitment failures by diversifying spawning effort across time.

The earliest life stages of Scarus rubroviolaceus are characterized by a remarkably small size at the onset of exogenous life. The wet weight at birth, based on an egg diameter of 0.75 mm typical of chaetodontid and labrid fishes, is estimated at 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams]. This minimal initial mass reflects the pelagic spawning strategy of the species, where numerous small, buoyant eggs are released into the water column. Following fertilization, the embryos develop within a yolk-laden, transparent chorion, sustaining the lecithotrophic larva until the onset of exogenous feeding. The tiny hatchling must navigate a planktonic environment rich in predators and poor in predictable food patches, making the early larval period a severe demographic bottleneck. Mortality during this phase is exceptionally high, yet the production of vast numbers of offspring from repeatedly spawning adults compensates for the losses. The transition from a yolk-dependent larva to an actively feeding, exotrophic larva represents a critical physiological shift that determines cohort strength.

Longevity data for the Ember parrotfish are derived from otolith-based age estimations conducted on a population inhabiting a thermally stable reef system. The maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years], achieved under the prevailing water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This extended lifespan, spanning roughly two decades, places Scarus rubroviolaceus among the longer-lived members of its genus and is typical of large-bodied, late-maturing scarids. The species' slow life history, characterized by a late age at maturation and a long reproductive window, contrasts sharply with smaller, more fecund reef fishes that exhibit rapid turnover. Age-related mortality increases markedly after the second decade, and individuals exceeding twenty years are rarely encountered in survey catches. The capacity for repeated annual spawning over such a prolonged period underscores the importance of protecting older, larger individuals within the population, as they contribute disproportionately to lifetime reproductive output and to the stability of the reef ecosystem through their bioerosion activities.
